description_full: International Seaways, Inc. owns and operates a fleet of oceangoing vessels for the transportation of crude oil and petroleum products in the international flag trade. The company operates in two segments: Crude Tankers and Product Carriers. It operates fleet of 70 vessels of VLCCs, Suezmaxes, and Aframaxes, as well as MRs, LR1, and LR2 product carrier. The company provides ship-to-ship (STS) lightering support services, such as hoses and fenders; and full-service STS lightering that includes lightering vessels. It also offers MR product carriers, including IMO III compliant for carrying edible oils, such as palm and vegetable oil, increasing flexibility when switching between cargo grades. The company serves independent and state-owned oil companies, oil traders, refinery operators, and international government entities. The company was formerly known as OSG International, Inc. and changed its name to International Seaways, Inc. in October 2016. International Seaways, Inc. was incorporated in 1999 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: International Seaways, Inc. is a mid-cap energy business with a $5.0B market cap on $843M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding. Operating margins are expanding by +4.4pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 8% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $379M in free cash flow — roughly 45 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.23× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.1×.

Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 14% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 3.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
